title: Gleaning (Ruth 2)
hook: Ruth gathers leftover grain, and Boaz tells his workers to drop some on purpose

segments.voice: Yesterday, Naomi and whither thou goest, and your line was where you go, I go. Did you show up for the person you named, even in a small way? Day seven hundred eight.

Barley harvest in Bethlehem. Two widows have come home with no husbands and nothing to eat, and the younger one makes a plan. "Let me now go to the field, and glean ears of corn." Corn in the old English just means grain. To glean is to walk behind the reapers and pick up what they drop: the stray stalks, the bits at the edges. It's the work of people with nothing. So Ruth, a foreigner, goes out alone to somebody else's field. And the storyteller says, almost with a wink, "her hap was to light on a part of the field belonging unto Boaz," a relative of Naomi's dead husband. Her hap. It just happened. Then Boaz himself walks out from town and greets his workers, "The LORD be with you," and they answer, "The LORD bless thee."
screen: `LET ME NOW GO TO THE FIELD.`
`HER HAP WAS TO LIGHT ON BOAZ'S FIELD.`

segments.voice: Ruth isn't stealing, and she isn't begging. She's using a law. In Leviticus, God tells Israel: "thou shalt not wholly reap the corners of thy field, neither shalt thou gather the gleanings of thy harvest." Leave them, it says, for the poor and the stranger. Deuteronomy adds the sheaf you forgot in the field: don't go back for it; it shall be for the stranger, for the fatherless, and for the widow. Ruth is two of those three at once. The law built a margin into every farm, so the hungry could feed themselves with their own hands. Boaz notices her and asks who she is. He tells her to stay in his field, near his young women, and says he's told the young men not to touch her. Ruth falls on her face and asks the question of the whole chapter: "Why have I found grace in thine eyes, that thou shouldest take knowledge of me, seeing I am a stranger?" He's heard what she did for Naomi, he says, and he blesses her, under the God of Israel, "under whose wings thou art come to trust." Then comes the line this day turns on. When she gets up to glean, Boaz quietly tells his reapers: "let fall also some of the handfuls of purpose for her, and leave them, that she may glean them, and rebuke her not." The law said leave the edges and what drops. Boaz goes past the law: drop more, on purpose, and don't say a word. Ruth never has to ask for more. She simply finds more than she expected. That evening she beats out what she gathered, and the text says it was about an ephah of barley. Naomi sees it and asks where she worked. Hearing the name Boaz, the bitter widow from yesterday says, "Blessed be he of the LORD, who hath not left off his kindness to the living and to the dead."
screen: `THE LAW LEFT THE EDGES FOR STRANGERS.`
`WHY ME, SEEING I AM A STRANGER?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: leave something on purpose for someone. Settle, and breathe. Think through the rest of your day and look for the edges of your field: a little extra time, money, food, attention, a parking spot, the last slice. Pick one thing you could leave behind, quietly, for someone who could use it, in a way that lets them simply find it, the way Ruth found the handfuls. No speech, no credit. If you pray, you can hold that person in prayer as you decide. The bell holds the time.
Gleaning. Gathering what the reapers leave behind. The law left the edges of the field for the poor and the stranger, and Boaz left more.
Your line: drop some on purpose. Today, leave the thing you picked where someone can find it, and don't tell anyone it was you. Day seven hundred eight.

howItsDone: Christians read Ruth 2 together with the gleaning laws of Leviticus and Deuteronomy, and some churches and charities name food-rescue work, gathering surplus harvest for people in need, after gleaning.

myth: Ruth gleans by begging Boaz for grain
she uses a law that left the edges and the dropped grain for the poor and the stranger.
Boaz tells his reapers to drop extra grain on purpose
"let fall also some of the handfuls of purpose for her" (Ruth 2:16).
Naomi is angry when she hears Ruth worked in Boaz's field
she says, blessed be he of the LORD, who hath not left off his kindness to the living and to the dead (Ruth 2:20).

fork.setup: you're Boaz. a foreign widow is gleaning in your field behind your workers. you've heard how loyal she's been. what do you do?
options: give her a sack of grain in front of everyone.
tell your reapers to drop handfuls for her on purpose, and say nothing.
follow the law, and leave the corners as usual.
fork.reveal: Boaz tells them to let handfuls fall of purpose and to rebuke her not (Ruth 2:16). she finds more than she expected.

original.note: Hebrew: to glean, to gather up. the verb behind Ruth's gleaning all through Ruth 2.

trapdoor: what you thought: gleaning, picking up scraps.
what it means: a right the law gave the poor and the stranger, to the edges and the dropped grain of every field.
what a scholar hears: Leviticus 19:9–10 and Deuteronomy 24:19 behind Ruth 2, and Boaz going past them with handfuls let fall on purpose (2:16).

notes: 'About an ephah of barley' is Ruth 2:17.
Ruth 'two of those three' (stranger and widow) refers to the list in Deuteronomy 24:19.
Original: לָקַט (lah-KAHT), the root of the gleaning verb in Ruth 2 (e.g. 2:2 וַאֲלַקֳטָה). Confirm form and pronunciation.
howItsDone mentions churches and charities that name food-rescue work after gleaning, with no count; confirm this is acceptable or cut.
The gleaning law is presented positively, as a provision of the Torah, not as a foil for Boaz; 'Boaz goes past the law' means he gives beyond its minimum.
Audit: "Ruth never has to be handed charity" contradicted Ruth 2:14, where Boaz reaches her parched corn at mealtime; now "Ruth never has to ask for more".

Editor: cut 'no land' from the hook (Ruth 4:3 says Naomi has a parcel of land to sell); Naomi's response now quotes Ruth 2:20 exactly, since the KJV has her blessing Boaz ('blessed be he of the LORD') and it is ambiguous whose kindness has not left off; myth reveal changed to match.
